full_judgment:
2. The short facts are that on 21st Shraban, corresponding to 6.8.76 the accused appellants being armed with various deadly weapons by forming an unlawful assembly entered the disputed land, measuring 10 kathas of land from north south of plot No. 462 under Khatian No. 37 of mouza Poradaha under Mirpur P.S., District Kushtia and cut and took away ripe Aush Paddy grown by the complainant through his bargader Jhomour Ali, causing a loss of Taka 1,000/- The further case of the complainant is that the disputed portion of plot No 462 of khatian No. 37 fell in his saham on partition. After examining the complainant on oath the learned Magistrate having found a prima facie case summoned the accused under section 379 of the Penal Code and Criminal Case No. 1081 of 1976 was started. The defence case was that they were falsely implicated in this case of paddy cutting as in fact the disputed land belonged to them by way of purchase under a registered sale deed from Fuljan, the original owner of the land and in pursuance of the said sale they were inducted into possession of the disputed land and that their possession is evidenced by the entry in the settlement record with regard to this land. They categorically insisted that they cut their own paddy, grown by them on their own land acquired by them legally for valid consideration and there could not be any question of taking away paddy from the ownership or possession of the complainant dishonestly. Before the prosecuting Magistrate, the prosecution examined as many as 6 witnesses to substantiate the prosecution case. The defence examined none but proved into evidence a number of documents in support of their defence. The learned Magistrate on an appraisal of the evidence on record found the accused appellants guilty under section 379 of the Penal Code and sentenced all of them thereunder to suffer rigorous imprisonment for a period of 3 months each. The accused appellants preferred an appeal before the learned Sessions Judge but the said appeal was dismissed, confirming the decision of the trial Court. As against that the petitioner has moved this Court under sections 435 and 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and had obtained this Rule calling upon the Deputy Commissioner. Kushtia and opposite party No. 1 Khoshlal, to show cause as to why the order of conviction and sentence complained of should not be set aside. Pending hearing of the Rule the appellants were enlarged on bail to the satisfaction of the Deputy Commissioner, Kushtia. 

 3. In a case under section 379 of the Penal Code the prosecution is to prove beyond all reasonable doubts that the subject matter of the theft is a movable property that it was in his or their possession which the accused moved without the consent of the person in possession, with the intention of taking it out of possession of such person dishonestly here is an element of mens rea. There must exist a dishonest mind in cutting dishonestly at the time of so removing from the possession of the owner in order to cause wrongful gain to the taker thereof and corresponding wrongful loss to the possessor thereof. Mere taking away something honestly on a bonafide belief of right today and then appropriating the same the next day even dishonestly may not amount to thieving. Further under the provisions of the Penal Code as existed in this country a person can even be convicted of stealing of his own property if he takes the same dishonestly from the lawful possession of another. Hence, as dishonesty is one of the essential ingredients of the offence of theft, possession of the property stolen is another essential ingredient of the offence of theft. The said question of possession is not a question of title as even an owner can be convicted of stealing of his own property from the lawful possession of another. If the property, alleged to have been stolen, was removed from the possession of one person who may not even be the rightful owner of the same but having a right to hold the same against the owner there would be a theft. A person may remove lawfully a thing either because it was in his possession or because he had a bonafide title to it which claim was not a mere presence of a bonafide claim. Keeping this in view it will be seen that in a case of theft of crop it is necessary for a Court to find out who was in actual possession of the crop in question at the time of taking and who had actually grown the crop on the land as in a case of theft of crop the subject matter of the offence would be the crop and not the land on which it was grown and bonafide claim of right thus would be preferable to the subject matter of the alleged offence which in the instant case was the ripe grown paddy. The complainant's case was that they obtained possession of the property on which the paddy was grown by means of an amicable partition but on a reference to the evidence on record it is seen that the complainant has admitted that the said partition, suit was only at the preliminary stage and had not been made final but he had obtained possession of the disputed land not through the Court but through a village Salish as to which Salish there is no evidence on record and there was no finding of the said on either way by any of the Courts below. This goes at the root of the plaintiffs claim of ownership of the land in question which is however not the subject matter of the present case. The defence has admitted into evidence a copy of the settlement record which clearly recorded the names of the accused’s against the disputed land as a tenant. An entry in the khatian is not an evidence of title but it is an evidence of possession unless it is rebut-ted by admissible evidence. Hence, there is evidence on record to show that it was the accused and not the complainant who was in possession of the land in question. This entry in the khatian in the name of the accused has not at all been considered by any of the Courts below for the purpose of a finding as to possession. 

 4. On a reference to the plaintiffs case it is apparent that it was never the plaintiffs case that he actually had grown the paddy as it was the allegation that he was in possession of the paddy but grown by his bargadars. The word "possession" has not been defined in the Code. Section 27 of the Penal Code, however, deals with a property in the possession of a person's wife, clerk or servant "on account of that person" and if so possessed by a person's wife, his clerk or his servant, it would be deemed to be in that person's possession within the meaning of the Code, which is analogous to "custody". Thus, the term possession, when interpreted in the light of section 27 of the Penal Code it would appear that possession of a servant, wife or clerk would be a possession on account of their master which master would be competent to take the same from the custody of those persons at will. In the instant case it is stated that his bargadars had shown the paddy and if that be so, could it be said that the bargadar were holding the entire aman crop on account of his master or that the plaintiff was possessing the crop of his bargadars. The answer is in the negative for the simple reason that a bargadar only pays the barga crops to his landlord but grown by the bargadars and he is neither a servant nor a clerk of his landlord but a free agent and not a custodian. In the instant case the person who actually had grown the paddy, even according to the complainant, did not file any complaint but it was filed by a person who neither had grown nor in possession as owner which it will be evident on reference to the evidence. P.W. 5 Jhomur Ali, aged about 60 years and allegedly the bargadar, of the complainant deposed to say that he himself cultivated the area of the land and he himself had sown the Aman paddy and the accused had taken away "my paddy" out of that land. He further deposed to say that he never saw the occurrence of the said taking away by the accuseds. P.W. 4 deposed to say that Jhamur Ali cultivated the land which the accused took away stating further that previously the land used to be cultivated by the complainant. It is seen from the evidence of these two witnesses that neither of them deposed to say that Motleb, the complainant, had grown the paddy which were allegedly taken away by the complainant. Further P. W. 4 categorically stated that Motleb used to cultivate previously the land in question but he has sown this year the paddy in question, P. W. 2 Hamed Ali, a brother of the complainant Motleb, deposed to say that the complainant took away the ripe paddy belonging to the complainant but sown by his brother's bargadars. On a reference to the evidence of these witnesses it is thus seen that the assertion of the complain-ant that he had obtained the suit land through a village salish, while the partition suit was still pending, had been corroborated by any of the witnesses and it is further seen that both P.W. 3 and P.W. 4 had categorically deposed to say that previously this land was cultivated by the complainant himself but not during the year when the occurrence took place. It was categorical defence plea that complainant never went into possession of the land in question but rather they were the owner of the land by purchase and were in possession of the same as owner by cultivating the same themselves as evidenced by the entry in the khatian as to possession of the land and title to the land as evidenced by sale deed in question and the said plea could not be disproved by the complainant by admissible evidence, as none of his witnesses deposed to say that he was in actual physical possession and actually grown the paddy in question.
